the 14-base and 77-base deletions are the molecular basis of the MPO defect, the 14- and 77-base-deleted mRNA are the molecular basis for the MPO defect in the father and in the daughter, respectively, and the MPO gene in the daughter is switched off at an early differentiation stage.

the molecular basis of hereditary myeloperiodase deficiency is the 14-base-pair deletion, and that the 14-base pair deletion can be associated to different mRNA phenotypes depending on the differentiation stage of the cell.

the 14-base MPO deletion in the father and in his daughter, which is located in a different exon of the gene, is responsible for the absence of the enzyme in the father's neutropilic granules and for the generation of a truncated MPO mRNA in the daughter's granulocyte precurosors.
In summary, our research is concerned with

a new type of genetic defect in MPO deficiency, in which the same mutation can be expressed with different phenotypes depending on the genetic context and on the stage of granulopoietic differentiation.
the biochemical and molecular characterization of a rare case of hereditary MPO deficiency, which is the first case of MPO deficiency in which a molecular defect has been identified.
the molecular mechanisms that regulate the expression of a human gene, the MPO gene, in normal and pathological situations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the father has a MPO deficiency caused by two mutations (T --> C transition, M251T, and 14-base deletion) in the MPO gene, whereas the daughter has a MPO defect caused by the 77-base mRNA deletion, resulting from the 14 base-deletion in the MPO cDNA, and by a MPO gene switch-off mutation.
the 14-base mutation is responsible for the absence of MPO in the father, whereas the MPO deficiency of the daughter is caused by a combination of the 14- and the 77-base mutations.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in the father the 14-base deleted allele was not transcribed, while in the daughter the same allele was transcribed but the mRNA was degraded, and in the mother the wild-type allele was expressed.

the MPO gene defect in the daughter is the result of two mutations: the 14-base insertion in exon 9 and an unknown regulatory mutation, whereas the MPO gene in the father has only the 14-base mutation.

The main takeaway from our work is that
a single genetic defect can be expressed in different ways in the same individual, as well as in different individuals, depending on the genetic background and on the differentiation state.
MPO deficiency may be caused by different molecular mechanisms, including mutations in the gene, mutations in the promoter region, or mutations affecting the splicing process.
the study of MPO deficiency is a good model for the study of the mechanisms that control gene expression during granulocyte differentiation.
